passage: On Monday the teacher said the model project was due in two weeks, and Harsha felt only a warm wave of relief. Two weeks! That was almost forever. Zainab, at the next desk, was already planning her volcano. Harsha drew spaceships in the margin instead. Days went by, one, four, seven. At the end of the first week Harsha thought, still lots of time. On the tenth day, a small pinch in the stomach. On the twelfth, Harsha realised the day after tomorrow was tomorrow. The last two evenings were a blur of glue, cardboard and a very tired mother, and the model went in slightly lopsided but finished.

qa.q: How long did the teacher give for the model project?
qa.a: The teacher said the model project was due in two weeks.

qa.q: What did Harsha feel when the teacher announced two weeks?
qa.a: Harsha felt a warm wave of relief, sure there was almost forever, so the deadline had no emotional weight yet.

qa.q: What could Harsha do at the start of the two weeks to avoid the last-two-day rush?
qa.a: Choose a small first job for the first week, like making a sketch or listing the materials, and write a mid-way date on the calendar.

qa.q: How might Zainab see the difference between the two of them?
qa.a: Zainab, already planning a volcano, probably sees that the project has become real for Zainab and may wonder why Harsha is drawing spaceships.

grounding: A child told a project is due in two weeks feels there is endless time and does nothing until the last two days.

passage:
“It's due in two weeks, Papa. That's ages,” said Tanvir, not looking up from the tablet.
“Two weeks is fourteen days,” said Baljeet. “What will you do on the first one?”
“Nothing. I'll do it later.”
Days passed. On the twelfth evening, Baljeet found Tanvir sitting on the floor with cardboard, scissors and no plan.
“How did that happen?” Baljeet asked.
“I thought I had so much time. Two weeks was so long.”
“And now?”
“Now it's two days.” Tanvir's voice cracked. “Can you help me hold this?”
Baljeet knelt on the floor beside him. “I'll hold it. You decide what goes where.”

qa.q: On which evening did Baljeet find Tanvir with cardboard and scissors?
qa.a: Baljeet found Tanvir on the twelfth evening.

qa.q: How does Tanvir feel when the voice cracks and the project is two days away?
qa.a: Tanvir feels panicky and ashamed, and his voice cracking shows the deadline has finally become real.

qa.q: What could Baljeet and Tanvir do so the next project does not end this way?
qa.a: Write the due date on the wall, and split the two weeks into small steps with a first task on day one.

qa.q: How might Baljeet feel kneeling beside Tanvir?
qa.a: Baljeet is probably concerned and patient, willing to hold the cardboard but leaving the decisions to Tanvir.

grounding: A child told a project is due in two weeks feels there is endless time and begins only in the last days.

passage: Nazia, listen, your Bua, Parul, was just like you at nine. Her teacher gave the class two weeks to make a model of a village well. Two weeks! To her, that was forever. I'm your Dadi and her mother, and I remember her saying, "There's so much time, Amma, I'll do it next week." Next week became "after Sunday". Then, on the second-last evening, she came running to me in tears. No clay, no straws, and the shop was closing. We ran together in the rain. She stayed up late pressing wet clay while I held the torch. The well leaned to one side. She still keeps a photo of that crooked well.

qa.q: What model did Parul have to make?
qa.a: She had to make a model of a village well.

qa.q: What was Parul feeling on the second-last evening?
qa.a: She felt panicked and upset, running to Dadi in tears with no clay or straws.

qa.q: What choice in the story could have changed how it ended?
qa.a: If Parul had bought the clay and straws in the first week, instead of saying "next week", she wouldn't have had to rush in the rain.

qa.q: How did Dadi experience Parul's last-minute rush?
qa.a: Dadi ran through the rain to the shop and held the torch late into the night, supporting Parul through a rush that could have been avoided.

grounding: An elder tells how a child given two weeks for a project felt there was endless time and did nothing until the last evenings.

passage: Avni, ten, was told on the first of the month that her solar system project was due on the fifteenth. "Two whole weeks," she told her friend Nilesh, and went back to playing hopscotch. Then her grandmother fell ill, and the family spent three days at the hospital in the town. When Avni got home, it was the twelfth. Her mother was still at the hospital, and there were no thermocol balls in the house. Avni sat with the blank chart, her stomach churning. Nilesh brought over his old balls and helped her paint. She finished on the fourteenth at midnight, with Saturn missing its ring.

qa.q: When was Avni's project due?
qa.a: It was due on the fifteenth.

qa.q: What was Avni feeling when she sat with the blank chart?
qa.a: She felt anxious, with her stomach churning, realising there was almost no time left.

qa.q: What could Avni have done to protect herself from surprises?
qa.a: She could have started in the first week, even a little, so that a family emergency wouldn't have pushed everything to the last days.

qa.q: How might Nilesh feel helping Avni paint at the last minute?
qa.a: Nilesh probably felt kind and a bit hurried, sharing his old balls to help a friend in trouble.

grounding: Shows a child treating a two-week deadline as endless time until a family emergency leaves only the last days.

passage: In their Kochi apartment, Thomas, eleven, had a two-week deadline for a scrapbook on local birds. His mother pinned the date on the fridge. "Plenty of time," he said, and went cycling with his neighbour Ishita every evening. The fridge note became part of the wallpaper. On the Friday before the Monday deadline, Ishita mentioned she had pasted her last picture. Thomas froze. He had four photos and no captions. All weekend he worked, cutting and writing, while Ishita cycled alone. On Sunday night he finished, eyes gritty. "Two weeks felt like forever," he told his mother, "until it was two days."

qa.q: What was Thomas's scrapbook about?
qa.a: It was a scrapbook on local birds.

qa.q: How did Thomas feel when Ishita mentioned her last picture?
qa.a: He froze, feeling shocked and panicky, realising he had only four photos and no captions.

qa.q: What could help Thomas next time a deadline seems far away?
qa.a: Breaking it into small tasks with dates, such as photos in week one and captions in week two, so the distant deadline feels real sooner.

qa.q: What is it like for Ishita when Thomas has to work all weekend?
qa.a: Ishita ends up cycling alone, missing her friend while he rushes to catch up.

grounding: Shows a child feeling there is endless time for a two-week project until only the last two days remain.

passage:
"Two weeks for the bird scrapbook!" Ganga said at dinner. "That's forever."
"You need drawings and a page for each bird," said Shreya, passing the rice. "Want to do the cover tonight?"
"Tonight? Didi, it's not even due till the twentieth."
Twelve days later:
"Shreya didi, where's the glue stick? Where are the crow feathers?"
"You collected feathers?"
"I was going to." Ganga's voice wobbled. "It's due the day after tomorrow and I've done one page."
"Okay. Breathe. Which birds can you see from our balcony?"
"Pigeons. Mynas. The kingfisher at the lake."
"Then that's three pages by bedtime. Go."
Ganga grabbed the colour pencils, sniffing. "Why didn't it feel close before?"

qa.q: What was Ganga's project?
qa.a: A bird scrapbook.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling twelve days later, and what shows it?
qa.a: Ganga was panicked and upset: the voice wobbled, Ganga was sniffing, and only one page was done with the scrapbook due in two days.

qa.q: What could Ganga take from Shreya's first suggestion for the next project?
qa.a: Doing a small piece, like the cover, on the very first night would make the deadline feel real early and leave less for the last days.

qa.q: How might Shreya feel during the last-minute rush?
qa.a: Shreya is probably a little frustrated after offering help on the first night, but also sympathetic, which is why she calms Ganga and makes a simple plan.

grounding: Shows a child who treats a two-week deadline as endless time and only feels its weight in the last two days.
